title: Lower-Intensity Training Day
description: Sleep and/or cardiovascular recovery signals are modestly below your personal baseline — not enough to call a recovery deficit, but enough to favor easier training today. Recommends swapping planned hard training for Zone 1/2 cardio, walking, or mobility work instead of cancelling training outright.
source: Huberman Lab (training/recovery balance); product heuristic (trigger combination)

conditional.question: Is your recovery looking a little off today (sleep or HRV slightly down)?

actions.action: Swap hard training for Zone 1/2 cardio, walking, or mobility
actions.frequency: Once, on the day this triggers
actions.details: Keep the training session, but drop the intensity: easy aerobic pace, a walk, or a mobility/stretching session instead of intervals, heavy lifting, or a max-effort workout. This is a downgrade, not a cancellation.

benefits: Keeps the training habit intact on a borderline-recovery day instead of an all-or-nothing skip
Avoids adding meaningful cardiovascular/sympathetic load on top of an already-softer recovery signal
Lower stakes than delaying training outright — appropriate for a single or loosely-corroborated signal
science: A single moderately depressed HRV reading, or a looser two-signal combination of reduced sleep duration and elevated resting heart rate, is a weaker and less specific indicator of reduced recovery capacity than a concurrent three-signal deviation. At this confidence level the evidence-based response is to favor easier training modalities rather than treating it as a hard stop, consistent with general training-load-management guidance (train through minor recovery dips at reduced intensity, reserve full rest for stronger/more corroborated signals).
contraindications: Not a reason to skip training altogether at this tier — signal is single or loosely corroborated
If this triggers on most days, the underlying baseline itself may be shifting (e.g. new training block, illness onset, life stress) — worth a broader look rather than only reacting day to day

learning_resources.title: Foundations of Fitness: Structuring Workouts Optimally — Huberman Lab

evidence_metadata.scientific_rationale: Single-signal (HRV < 92% baseline) OR a looser two-signal combination (sleep duration < 93% baseline AND resting HR > 103% baseline), for one night. Deliberately looser than the recovery-deficit 'mild' tier (docs/oura-rules/recovery-deficit.json, 90%/90% two-signal sleep_duration+HRV) — this rule uses a different metric pairing and an OR-of-groups shape so it can fire on a single moderately-off HRV reading alone, trading specificity for earlier/cheaper action (a training-intensity swap, not a recovery protocol).

evidence_for_protocol.notes: Favoring lower-intensity training (easy aerobic work, mobility) over hard training on days with softer recovery signals, while still training, is a standard and directly-supported training-load-management principle discussed in Huberman Lab's fitness content — this is a milder version of the same logic as the existing 'reduce high-intensity training' action in the recovery-deficit high tier.

evidence_for_trigger.notes: The 92%/93%/103% thresholds, the single-vs-two-signal OR structure, and the choice of HRV alone as a sufficient single trigger are product heuristics, not independently validated. Chosen to sit clearly below the recovery-deficit mild tier in both specificity and stakes (a same-workout intensity swap, not an NSDR recommendation or training cancellation) so a false positive costs almost nothing.

expected_effect.short_term: Marginally lower same-day cardiovascular/sympathetic load from training; unlikely to be measurable on the ring within 24h.
expected_effect.long_term: May reduce the frequency of escalation into the recovery-deficit or delay-hard-training tiers by catching softer dips earlier, though untested.
